--- title: "Lesson 18: Two-Sample Confidence Intervals and Tests for Means" subtitle: "BSTA 551: Statistical Inference" author: "Jessica Minnier" title-slide-attributes: data-background-color: "#006a4e" date: "2026-03-02" format: revealjs: theme: "../simple_NW.scss" chalkboard: true scrollable: true slide-number: true show-slide-number: all width: 1955 height: 1100 footer: Lesson 18 - Two-Sample Inference for Means html-math-method: mathjax highlight-style: atom-one execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- # Lesson 18: Two-Sample Inference for Means {background-color="#2c3e50"} ## Review: Where We Left Off **Lessons 15–17: Hypothesis Testing** - Neyman-Pearson Lemma: MP tests via likelihood ratio - Likelihood Ratio Tests (LRT) for composite hypotheses - Bootstrap hypothesis tests: shift data to satisfy $H_0$, approximate null distribution - Permutation tests (preview) . . . **Today's Goals:** 1. Extend one-sample inference to **two independent samples** 2. Derive and apply the two-sample **z-test and CI** (variances known) 3. Derive and apply the **Welch t-test** (variances unknown, unequal) 4. Understand the **pooled t-test** (variances assumed equal) and when it is appropriate 5. Connect CIs and tests via the duality theorem 6. Apply all methods to medical research examples ## Roadmap | Setting | Variances | Test Statistic | Reference | |---------|-----------|---------------|-----------| | Two independent samples | $\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2$ known | $Z$ | DBC 9.5 | | Two independent samples | $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ unknown | Pooled $T$ | DBC 9.5 | | Two independent samples | $\sigma_1^2 \neq \sigma_2^2$ unknown | Welch $T$ | DBC 9.5 | . . . ::: callout-note ## Motivating Example A clinical trial randomizes $n_1 = 45$ patients to a new antihypertensive drug and $n_2 = 43$ to placebo. After 12 weeks, we measure the reduction in systolic blood pressure (mmHg). **Does the drug produce a larger mean reduction than placebo?** We need two-sample methods because the groups are **independent**. ::: # Two-Sample Setup and Point Estimation {background-color="#3498db"} ## The Two-Sample Model **Setup:** Two independent random samples from possibly different populations: $$X_{11}, X_{12}, \ldots, X_{1n_1} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_1 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_1, \text{ variance } \sigma_1^2$$ $$X_{21}, X_{22}, \ldots, X_{2n_2} \stackrel{iid}{\sim} F_2 \quad \text{with mean } \mu_2, \text{ variance } \sigma_2^2$$ The two samples are **independent of each other**. . . . **Parameter of interest:** $\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ **Point estimator:** $\hat{\Delta} = \bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2$ . . . **Properties of $\hat{\Delta}$:** - $E[\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2] = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ $\Rightarrow$ **unbiased** - $\text{Var}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}$ (by independence) - SE$(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}$ ## Sampling Distribution of $\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2$ **Case 1: Both populations normal** (any sample size): $$\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)$$ **Case 2: Non-normal populations, large samples** (CLT): $$\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\; \frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}\right)$$ . . . In either case, the standardized statistic is approximately $N(0,1)$: $$Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1)$$ This is a **pivotal quantity** when $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are known. # Case 1: Variances Known (z-procedures) {background-color="#e74c3c"} ## Two-Sample z-Interval (DBC 9.5) When $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are **known**, the pivot $Z$ gives a $100(1-\alpha)\%$ CI for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$: $$(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}$$ . . . **Two-sample z-test** of $H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = \Delta_0$: $$Z = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2}}$$ Reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$: | Alternative | Rejection Region | |-------------|-----------------| | $\mu_1 - \mu_2 > \Delta_0$ | $Z > z_\alpha$ | | $\mu_1 - \mu_2 < \Delta_0$ | $Z < -z_\alpha$ | | $\mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq \Delta_0$ | $|Z| > z_{\alpha/2}$ | ## Medical Example: Two-Sample z-Test **Study:** A pilot study compares mean serum cortisol (μg/dL) between ICU patients with sepsis ($n_1 = 30$, known $\sigma_1 = 6$) and non-septic ICU controls ($n_2 = 35$, known $\sigma_2 = 5$). Observed: $\bar{x}_1 = 28.4$, $\bar{x}_2 = 22.1$. Test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs. $H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Summary statistics xbar1 <- 28.4; xbar2 <- 22.1 sigma1 <- 6; sigma2 <- 5 n1 <- 30; n2 <- 35 alpha <- 0.05 # Test statistic and p-value (one-sided) se_diff <- sqrt(sigma1^2/n1 + sigma2^2/n2) z_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / se_diff p_value <- pnorm(z_obs, lower.tail = FALSE) # 95% CI (two-sided) z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2) ci_lo <- (xbar1 - xbar2) - z_crit * se_diff ci_hi <- (xbar1 - xbar2) + z_crit * se_diff cat("SE of difference:", round(se_diff, 3), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SE of difference: 1.384 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("Z statistic:", round(z_obs, 3), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Z statistic: 4.553 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("One-sided p-value:", round(p_value, 5), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` One-sided p-value: 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("95% CI for mu1 - mu2: (", round(ci_lo, 2), ",", round(ci_hi, 2), ")\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 95% CI for mu1 - mu2: ( 3.59 , 9.01 ) ``` ::: ::: . . . **Conclusion:** $Z = 4.55$, $p < 0.001$. Strong evidence that septic ICU patients have higher mean cortisol. # Case 2: Variances Unknown {background-color="#27ae60"} ## The Challenge: Unknown Variances In practice, $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are **rarely known**. We estimate them from the data: $$S_1^2 = \frac{1}{n_1-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_1}(X_{1j}-\bar{X}_1)^2, \quad S_2^2 = \frac{1}{n_2-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_2}(X_{2j}-\bar{X}_2)^2$$ The standardized statistic $$T = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - (\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}$$ does **not** follow an exact $t$ distribution (Behrens-Fisher problem). . . . **Two approaches:** 1. **Welch (Satterthwaite) approximation**: $T$ is approximately $t_\nu$ with estimated df $\hat\nu$ 2. **Pooled t-test**: assume $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$, use exact $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$ distribution ## Welch's t-Test (DBC 9.5) — Recommended Default **Welch's t-statistic:** $$T_W = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{\sqrt{S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2}}$$ Under $H_0$, $T_W \approx t_{\hat\nu}$ where the **Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom** are: $$\hat\nu = \frac{(S_1^2/n_1 + S_2^2/n_2)^2}{\dfrac{(S_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1} + \dfrac{(S_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}$$ . . . **Welch 95% CI for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$:** $$(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,\hat\nu}\,\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}$$ ::: callout-important ## Why Welch? The Welch test is **robust** to unequal variances and performs well even when $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$. It is the default in R's `t.test()` and is recommended by most statisticians. ::: ## The Pooled t-Test (DBC 9.5) When $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = \sigma^2$ (equal variances), we pool information: $$S_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)S_1^2 + (n_2-1)S_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2} \quad \text{(pooled variance estimator)}$$ **Pooled t-statistic:** $$T_P = \frac{(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - \Delta_0}{S_p\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_2}} \sim t_{n_1+n_2-2} \quad \text{(exact, under normality + equal } \sigma^2\text{)}$$ . . . **Pooled 95% CI:** $$(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n_1+n_2-2}\;S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}$$ ::: callout-warning ## When to Use Pooled t Only use the pooled t when there is **strong prior reason** to believe $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ (e.g., same measurement in similar populations). Do not use an F-test on the same data to justify pooling — this inflates Type I error. ::: ## Welch vs. Pooled: Comparison ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(551) # Simulate 10,000 two-sample experiments under H0 # Compare Type I error when sigma1 != sigma2 sim_ttest <- function(n1, n2, sigma1, sigma2, B = 10000) { map_dfr(1:B, function(i) { x1 <- rnorm(n1, mean = 0, sd = sigma1) x2 <- rnorm(n2, mean = 0, sd = sigma2) p_welch <- t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value p_pooled <- t.test(x1, x2, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value tibble(p_welch = p_welch, p_pooled = p_pooled) }) } scenarios <- list( list(n1=20, n2=20, s1=2, s2=2, label="Equal n, Equal σ"), list(n1=20, n2=20, s1=1, s2=3, label="Equal n, σ1=1, σ2=3"), list(n1=10, n2=30, s1=1, s2=3, label="Small n₁, σ1=1, σ2=3 (n∝σ²)"), list(n1=30, n2=10, s1=1, s2=3, label="Large n₁, σ1=1, σ2=3 (n anti-∝σ²)") ) results <- map_dfr(scenarios, function(sc) { sim_ttest(sc$n1, sc$n2, sc$s1, sc$s2, B = 3000) |> summarise(Welch = mean(p_welch < 0.05), Pooled = mean(p_pooled < 0.05)) |> mutate(Scenario = sc$label) }) results |> pivot_longer(c(Welch, Pooled), names_to = "Test", values_to = "TypeI_Error") |> ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Scenario, -TypeI_Error), y = TypeI_Error, fill = Test)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.6) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Welch" = "#006a4e", "Pooled" = "#e74c3c")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.14), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) + labs( title = "Type I Error Rate: Welch vs. Pooled t-test (nominal α = 5%)", subtitle = "Dashed line = 5% target. Pooled test is anti-conservative when variances are unequal.", x = NULL, y = "Type I Error Rate", fill = "Method" ) + coord_flip() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18_TwoSample_Mean_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: ## Medical Example: Welch t-Test in R **RCT:** A randomized trial compares 12-week reduction in LDL cholesterol (mg/dL) between a statin drug ($n_1 = 45$) and placebo ($n_2 = 43$). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} set.seed(42) # Simulate individual-level data ldl_drug <- rnorm(45, mean = 32, sd = 18) # larger mean reduction ldl_placebo <- rnorm(43, mean = 8, sd = 12) # smaller reduction # Welch t-test (default in R) test_result <- t.test(ldl_drug, ldl_placebo, alternative = "greater", conf.level = 0.95) tidy(test_result) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 10 estimate estimate1 estimate2 statistic p.value parameter conf.low conf.high 1 21.3 30.8 9.52 5.97 5.39e-8 65.6 15.3 Inf # ℹ 2 more variables: method , alternative ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} tibble( reduction = c(ldl_drug, ldl_placebo), group = rep(c("Statin", "Placebo"), c(45, 43)) ) |> ggplot(aes(x = group, y = reduction, fill = group)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, width = 0.4) + geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Statin" = "#006a4e", "Placebo" = "#3498db")) + labs(title = "LDL Cholesterol Reduction by Treatment Group", subtitle = "Welch two-sample t-test", x = NULL, y = "LDL Reduction (mg/dL)", fill = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18_TwoSample_Mean_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Interpreting the Welch Output ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Two-sided CI for the difference (mu_drug - mu_placebo) ci_result <- t.test(ldl_drug, ldl_placebo, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95) cat("Welch df:", round(ci_result$parameter, 1), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch df: 65.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("Mean difference:", round(diff(rev(ci_result$estimate)), 2), "mg/dL\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mean difference: 21.25 mg/dL ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_result$conf.int[1], 2), ",", round(ci_result$conf.int[2], 2), ")\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 95% CI: ( 14.14 , 28.37 ) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat("p-value:", format.pval(ci_result$p.value, digits = 3), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` p-value: 1.08e-07 ``` ::: ::: . . . **Interpretation:** We estimate the statin reduces LDL by approximately 21.3 mg/dL more than placebo on average (95% CI: 14.1 to 28.4 mg/dL). This is highly statistically significant ($p < 0.001$, Welch t-test). ::: callout-note ## Report Both Always report both the **CI** (magnitude of effect) and the **p-value** (strength of evidence). Neither alone tells the full story. ::: ## Example: Pooled t-Test When Appropriate **Devore Example (DBC 9.5):** Two independent groups of adult male patients measured for systolic blood pressure: - Group 1 (standard care): $n_1 = 12$, $\bar{x}_1 = 140.2$, $s_1 = 14.3$ mmHg - Group 2 (intensive care): $n_2 = 10$, $\bar{x}_2 = 128.7$, $s_2 = 13.8$ mmHg Strong prior reason to assume equal population SDs (same measurement, similar populations). Test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs. $H_a: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} n1 <- 12; xbar1 <- 140.2; s1 <- 14.3 n2 <- 10; xbar2 <- 128.7; s2 <- 13.8 # Pooled variance sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2) sp <- sqrt(sp2) # Test statistic t_obs <- (xbar1 - xbar2) / (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)) df <- n1 + n2 - 2 # Two-sided p-value and 95% CI p_val <- 2 * pt(abs(t_obs), df = df, lower.tail = FALSE) t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = df) margin <- t_crit * sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) cat(sprintf("Pooled SD = %.2f, df = %d\n", sp, df)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pooled SD = 14.08, df = 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat(sprintf("T_obs = %.3f, p-value = %.4f\n", t_obs, p_val)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` T_obs = 1.908, p-value = 0.0709 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} cat(sprintf("95%% CI: (%.2f, %.2f)\n", xbar1 - xbar2 - margin, xbar1 - xbar2 + margin)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 95% CI: (-1.07, 24.07) ``` ::: ::: . . . **Conclusion:** $t = 1.908$, $df = 20$, $p = 0.0709$. At $\alpha = 0.05$, we reject $H_0$; evidence that systolic BP differs between care groups. ## Visualizing t-Distributions: Welch vs. Pooled ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # From the LDL example above n1_ldl <- 45; n2_ldl <- 43 s1_ldl <- sd(ldl_drug); s2_ldl <- sd(ldl_placebo) # Welch df nu_hat <- (s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl + s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl)^2 / ((s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl)^2/(n1_ldl-1) + (s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl)^2/(n2_ldl-1)) df_pooled_ldl <- n1_ldl + n2_ldl - 2 t_obs_ldl <- (mean(ldl_drug) - mean(ldl_placebo)) / sqrt(s1_ldl^2/n1_ldl + s2_ldl^2/n2_ldl) t_grid <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 500) df_plot <- bind_rows( tibble(t = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = round(nu_hat)), Distribution = sprintf("Welch (df=%.0f)", nu_hat)), tibble(t = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = df_pooled_ldl), Distribution = sprintf("Pooled (df=%d)", df_pooled_ldl)) ) ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = t, y = density, color = Distribution)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) + geom_vline(xintercept = t_obs_ldl, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) + annotate("text", x = t_obs_ldl + 0.3, y = 0.35, label = bquote(T[obs] == .(round(t_obs_ldl, 2))), color = "#e74c3c", size = 5, hjust = 0) + scale_color_manual(values = c("#006a4e", "#3498db")) + labs(title = "LDL Example: Welch vs. Pooled t-Distributions", subtitle = "With similar sample sizes and variances, the two distributions are nearly identical", x = "t", y = "Density", color = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18_TwoSample_Mean_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: # Sample Size and Power {background-color="#9b59b6"} ## Sample Size for Two-Sample t-Test For a two-sided test at level $\alpha$ with power $1 - \beta$ to detect $|\mu_1 - \mu_2| = \delta$ (assuming $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma$ and $n_1 = n_2 = n$): $$n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2(z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{\delta^2}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Clinical question: How many patients per arm to detect a 10 mmHg difference # in SBP with 90% power at alpha = 0.05 (two-sided)? sigma <- 15 # assumed common SD (mmHg) delta <- 10 # target difference to detect alpha <- 0.05 power <- 0.90 z_a2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2) z_b <- qnorm(power) n_per_arm <- ceiling(2 * sigma^2 * (z_a2 + z_b)^2 / delta^2) cat("Approximate n per arm:", n_per_arm, "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Approximate n per arm: 48 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Cross-check with power.t.test power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sigma, sig.level = alpha, power = power, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Two-sample t test power calculation n = 48.26431 delta = 10 sd = 15 sig.level = 0.05 power = 0.9 alternative = two.sided NOTE: n is number in *each* group ``` ::: ::: ## Summary: Which Two-Sample t-Test? ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # Key Takeaways {background-color="#2c3e50"} ## Key Takeaways ::: callout-important ## Today's Main Points (DBC 9.5) 1. **Point estimator:** $\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2$ is unbiased for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ with variance $\sigma_1^2/n_1 + \sigma_2^2/n_2$ 2. **z-procedures:** Use when $\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2$ known (or large samples approximation) 3. **Welch t-test** (recommended default): approximates the sampling distribution of the standardized difference with $t_{\hat\nu}$; the Welch-Satterthwaite df $\hat\nu$ accounts for unequal variances 4. **Pooled t-test:** Exact $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$ distribution under normality + $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$; requires strong prior justification for equal variances 5. **CI-test duality:** The 95% CI for $\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ contains all values of $\Delta_0$ for which the two-sided test would fail to reject at $\alpha = 0.05$ 6. **Always report** the estimated difference, its CI, and the p-value together ::: ## Looking Ahead **Next class: Two-Sample Inference for Proportions; Inferences About Two Variances** - $z$-test and CI for $p_1 - p_2$: comparing event rates between groups - F-test for equality of variances - Inferences about $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ . . . **Later: Paired Data (Lesson 20) and Bootstrap/Permutation for Two Samples (Lesson 21)** ## Homework 7 {.smaller} **Due:** March 5, 2026 at 11pm **Problem 1** (DBC 9.5 style): Two hospital units are compared on patient length of stay (days). Unit A ($n_1 = 20$, $\bar{x}_1 = 7.4$, $s_1 = 2.8$) vs. Unit B ($n_2 = 25$, $\bar{x}_2 = 6.1$, $s_2 = 3.5$). (a) Compute the Welch t-statistic and approximate df. (b) Construct a 95% Welch CI for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$. (c) Test $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ vs. $H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. State your conclusion. (d) Verify your answers using `t.test()` in R. **Problem 2** (DBC 9.5, pooled): Two formulations of an analgesic are tested for time to pain relief (minutes). Assume equal population SDs. Formulation A: $n_1 = 15$, $\bar{x}_1 = 48.3$, $s_1 = 8.1$. Formulation B: $n_2 = 15$, $\bar{x}_2 = 52.6$, $s_2 = 7.9$. (a) Compute $S_p^2$ and the pooled t-statistic. (b) Construct a 90% pooled CI for $\mu_A - \mu_B$. (c) What sample size per group would be needed to detect a 5-minute difference with 80% power at $\alpha = 0.05$? **Problem 3** (DBC 9.5): Using the cortisol example from class (sepsis vs. non-septic ICU patients), suppose $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are actually unknown. Re-analyze using: (a) Welch t-test. (b) Pooled t-test. (c) Compare results and discuss when conclusions might differ. ## References ::: nonincremental - Devore, Berk, and Carlton. *Modern Mathematical Statistics with Applications* (Springer). Section 9.5. - Welch, B. L. (1947). The generalization of 'Student's' problem when several different population variances are involved. *Biometrika*, 34(1–2), 28–35. ::: ## Questions? {.center background-color="#3498db"} Thank you!

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
